Thermoeconomic optimization of 
a hybrid power and cooling facility 
using waste heat recovery from a 
marine diesel engine
Mohamed Bechir Ben Hamida1, WaqidAl-Mussawi2, Mohamed Shaban3 & 
Mohammad Marefati4
Improving energy efficiency and reducing environmental impacts have become essential goals 
in today’s world. Finding ways to utilize waste heat for generating both power and cooling is a 
meaningful step toward more sustainable energy use and better resource management. In this 
research, the aim is to enhance the basic efficiency of diesel engines by harnessing the waste heat. 
By merging the diesel engine cycle with the ORC and the ejector-heat pipe cooling process, we can 
simultaneously generate power and cooling. This study focuses on tapping into the unused heat from 
a specific marine diesel engine to produce both power and cooling. The primary motivation is to cut 
down on fossil fuel usage due to its adverse environmental impact. To put it another way, this research 
focuses on increasing the base efficiency of diesel engines by recycling waste heat. By systematically 
integrating the diesel engine cycle with the organic Rankine cycle and the ejector-heat pipe cooling 
system, we can produce both power and cooling. Ultimately, 2-archive multi-objective cuckoo search 
algorithm-based optimization (MOCS2arc algorithm) establishes the optimized conceptual design. 
The system offers an electrical output of 72.01 kW and cooling capabilities of 56.83 kW, achieving an 
exergy efficiency of 60.4%. Moreover, economic metrics, including the facility’s unit cost of the product 
($1259/GJ) and annual exergy destruction costs ($386,670), were ascertained. Under the optimization, 
exergy efficacy and SUCP of 64.9% and $902.21/GJ are achievable.
Keywords Hybrid cooling and power, Waste heat recovery system, Marine diesel cycle, Exergoeconomic, 
2-archive multi-objective cuckoo search optimization algorithm
Today, energy stands as humanity’s most strategic need, and its provision has evolved into an ongoing concern 
for nations1–3. With the dwindling fossil fuel resources on one hand, and the adverse environmental effects they 
cause on the other, the importance and necessity of optimizing fossil fuel usage methods and energy production

becomes increasingly evident4,5. The rising consumption of fossil fuels, their limited availability, the steadily 
increasing cost of energy, and the environmental contamination emitted from the release of carbon dioxide 
and greenhouse gases, all strongly advocate for the efficient use of available energy and energy conservation6. 
Considering that the energy crisis is among the most fundamental challenges facing human societies, finding 
efficient energy production methods is a primary objective. Electricity production in thermal power plants is 
accompanied by significant losses7,8. Even under optimal production conditions, like those in a combined cycle, 
more than 50% of the input thermal energy does not get converted into electricity9,10. Instead, it is wasted as 
heat through plant smokestacks, plant condensers, and other equipment. Thus, the utilization of cogeneration 
systems emerges as a solution to reduce these losses and enhance the system’s efficiency11.
Cogeneration systems for simultaneous power, heat, and cooling serve as a solution to energy wastage 
and environmental challenges. By harnessing the maximum work, heat, and cooling produced from a single 
fuel source, these systems have attracted the attention of researchers. Such units employ a heat source and, by 
minimizing wasted energy, bring the system’s waste heat source temperature closer to ambient temperature,

thereby increasing the system’s thermal efficiency12,13. It is here that cogeneration systems for power, heat, and

cooling operate as an alternative system, satisfying diverse energy needs, ranging from cooling and heating to 
power. Given the significance of energy conversion topics in global advancement, effective utilization of energy 
resources and incorporating the industry of waste heat recovery can serve as suitable strategies for enhancing the 
efficiency and performance of cogeneration energy systems14,15.
Newly, there has been a heightened interest in recovering wasted heat, and researchers have proposed novel 
methods for power generation through high and medium-temperature heat sources. Among the methods 
proposed for power cycles, diesel engines owing to their features such as lower environmental pollution, 
economic feasibility16,17, high power, and elevated exhaust stream temperature can serve as an apt heat source 
in conjunction with other systems. Although, utilizing the marine engine waste heat potential that can be 
considered as a primary energy source for running power plan, very limited investigations have concentrated on 
the recovery of potential energy from the exhaust streams of internal combustion in mentioned type of engines18.
Agarwal et al.19 conducted an experimental research on agricultural machinery engines and power generators 
used the EGR method to study the pollution and performance of these engines. They concluded that with this 
method, the amount of NOX and the temperature of the exhaust gases decreased, but the levels of HC, CO, 
and particulate matter increased. In another investigation, researchers20, coupled two organic Rankine cycles 
(ORCs), one high-temperature and one low-temperature, using a heat exchanger, aiming to utilize the waste 
heat of engines. A waste heat recovery system for diesel engines was introduces by Song et al.21. In that study, 
two separate ORCs were used; one harnessed waste heat from the water chamber, and the other from exhaust gas 
emissions. For the appropriate fluid selection for each cycle and for optimizing system parameters, the highest 
power output generated by the system was set as the primary criterion. Moreover, by examining the results 
from the economic analysis and system design, they demonstrated that the system can be operational in real 
world. Zhao et al.22 conducted research on a co-generation power and heat system with a 70 kW gas-powered 
internal combustion engine in an office building in China. Scholars in another investigation23, conducted a

detailed assessment and optimization of the ORC system to harness waste heat from ship engine exhausts. The 
researchers mentioned that utilizing R141b in the optimized ORC setup offers a promising and cost-effective 
method for marine waste heat recovery.
Aghdoudchaboki et al.24 developed an integrated system for eco-friendly ships to harness waste heat from 
marine engines and produce both power and fresh water. Through a dual-objective optimization focused on 
exergy efficiency and total cost rate, an optimal condition was identified, boasting 35.96% exergy efficiency at a 
cost of $2.54/hr. To address the energy crisis and environmental pollution, Ouyang et al.25 focused on waste heat 
recovery from natural gas engines, given their environmental edge over diesel engines. A new system had been 
introduced that merges the supercritical CO2 Brayton cycle, a dual-effect cooling system using absorption, and 
the Kalina cycle for waste heat recovery. This system enhances power output by 15.33% and shortens the return 
on investment time by 25.6%. This makes it a viable method for capturing unused heat from natural gas motors.
Boodaghi et al.26 introduced a dual-loop Organic Rankine Cycle system aimed at recovering waste heat from 
a 12-cylinder stationary heavy-duty Diesel engine. A one-dimensional numerical model of the 1000 kW diesel 
engine was developed and subsequently validated against experimental data. The sensitivity analysis indicated 
that the total power output increases with higher values of the SOI, N, and elevated pressure in the hightemperature loop. Notably, the engine parameters did not influence the thermal efficiency or the rate of exergy 
destruction. In reference27, both normal and advanced exergy analyses of a waste heat recovery system were 
conducted. The proposed system features a dual-loop organic Rankine cycle designed to capture the waste heat 
available from the intake air. The total exergy destruction that could be avoided in the low-temperature loop was 
quantified at 46.62 kW, suggesting that it warrants greater focus compared to the high-temperature loop, which 
had a lower exergy destruction of 12.42 kW. Furthermore, Etghani and Boodaghi28 proposed a hybrid energy

system that utilizes solar energy, incorporating a parabolic trough collector, a supercritical CO2 Brayton cycle, 
a recuperative organic Rankine cycle, a proton exchange membrane electrolyzer, and a two-tank direct thermal 
energy storage system. This system is capable of delivering a dependable and sustainable supply of electricity, 
hydrogen, and hot water, showcasing a promising and feasible poly-generation technology suitable for both gridconnected and off-grid scenarios.
Avazpour et al.29 conducted a thorough study on a parallel ORC system designed to recover waste heat 
from diesel engines used in off-road applications. Their approach integrated both transcritical and subcritical 
operational modes. For optimization, they employed a multi-objective genetic algorithm, targeting both exergy 
efficiency and specific investment cost. Through this bi-objective optimization, they attained a peak exergy 
efficiency of 45.92%, paired with a specific investment cost of $3350/kW. In a related development, Lebedevas 
and Čepaitis30 numerically examined the practical considerations of ORC implementation with common marine 
medium-speed diesel engines, specifically citing the Wartsila 12V46F model. Their findings indicated that 
comprehensive waste heat recovery from all auxiliary heat sources within an ORC system could potentially boost 
the main engine’s energy efficiency by 13.5–21%. This efficiency gain was observed across a load range from 
100% down to 25% of the engine’s nominal power. Mahmoud et al.31 explored the use of a ground-cooled ORC 
system for recovering waste heat generated by a diesel generator. Their study utilized real-time experimental 
data for ambient and ground temperatures. The ORC system, when operating at a design temperature of 300 °C, 
resulted in a 7.98% increase in overall output power compared to operating the diesel generator in isolation.
In our research, we aim to enhance the basic efficiency of diesel engines by harnessing the waste heat. By 
merging the diesel engine cycle with the ORC and the ejector-heat pipe cooling process, we can simultaneously 
generate power and cooling. This study focuses on tapping into the unused heat from a specific marine diesel 
engine to produce both power and cooling. Our primary motivation is to cut down on fossil fuel usage due to

its adverse environmental impact. To put it another way, this research focuses on increasing the base efficiency 
of diesel engines by recycling waste heat. By systematically integrating the diesel engine cycle with the organic

Rankine cycle and the ejector-heat pipe cooling system, we can produce both power and cooling. Ultimately, 
2-archive multi-objective cuckoo search algorithm-based optimization (MOCS2arc algorithm) establishes the 
optimized conceptual design. The key differences and contributions of our study are now clearly articulated as 
follows:
i. While many existing studies focus on dual ORC loops or single-mode heat recovery, our work proposes 
a unique integration of an ORC with an ejector-heat pipe cooling subsystem, powered entirely by marine 
diesel exhaust. The use of a heat pipe allows passive circulation, eliminating the need for a mechanical pump, 
which reduces auxiliary energy consumption and improves reliability.
ii. Unlike most prior studies that focus on stationary engines or land-based systems, our research specifically 
targets marine diesel engines, which are underexplored despite their high thermal potential and continuous 
operation profiles.
iii. Our study applies the 2-Archive Multi-Objective Cuckoo Search (MOCS2arc) algorithm, which, compared 
to traditional multi-objective optimizers (e.g., NSGA-II, MOPSO), offers better convergence and diversity 
handling through its dual-archive approach. This ensures a more comprehensive and balanced trade-off 
between exergy efficiency and cost.
iv. Many previous works focus on either thermodynamic or simple economic assessments. We provide a detailed exergoeconomic breakdown, including cost of exergy destruction, component-level cost analysis, and 
sensitivity to key parameters, which is lacking in much of the existing literature.
Description of the proposed facility
In Fig. 1, we see a diagram showcasing the combined power and cooling system powered by a marine diesel 
engine. Table 1. provides the technical and functional details of this marine diesel engine. As illustrated, the 
heat produced from the engine’s exit first powers the ORC. After this, its remaining heat gets channelled to the

ejector-heat pipe cooling system. In this setup, the ORC, equipped with an inbuilt heat exchanger, is primarily 
designed for waste heat capture and boosting overall efficiency. Within the ORC, the organic fluid initially heads 
towards the internal heat exchanger. Here, by soaking up heat from the boiler sourced from the exhaust gas, it 
transforms into saturated steam. This heated fluid, due to its high temperature and pressure, propels the turbine, 
Fig. 1. scheme of the proposed combined cooling and power generation system.
Scientific Reports | (2025) 15:30810 | https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-16609-x 3
www.nature.com/scientificreports/
thereby generating power. Following this, the temperature of the stream that departs from the boiler drops as it 
releases its heat in the boiler, and then it advances to the cooling cycle’s generator. The cooling system consists of 
various components: a generator, ejector, a mock pump mimicking oscillatory movements inside the heat pipe, 
an expansion valve, a condenser, and lastly, an evaporator.
The fluid inside the generator gets heated from the exhaust gases and merges with the fluid coming from 
the evaporator before making its way to the ejector. Owing to the pressure disparity, the high-pressure and lowpressure streams combine in the ejector, resulting in a mid-level pressure. The outflow from the ejector then 
turns into a liquid. A fraction of this liquid utilizes the heat pipe’s oscillatory characteristic, simulating a pump 
to move into the generator. Concurrently, another segment experiences a drop in both pressure and temperature 
in the expansion valve, which consequently generates cooling in the evaporator.

The 2-archive multi-objective cuckoo search algorithm
The MOCS2arc algorithm is an advanced optimization technique designed to address complex multi-objective

problems by integrating the Cuckoo Search (CS) algorithm with a dual-archive strategy. The CS algorithm, 
inspired via the brood parasitism behavior of cuckoos, has been recognized for its effectiveness in global 
optimization tasks. The CS algorithm follows Lévy flight-based random walks to explore the search space 
efficiently. Mathematically, the position of a cuckoo is updated using:
xt+1
i = xt
i + α + L(λ ) (14)
where, α is the step size scaling factor and L(λ) represents a Lévy flight distribution given by:
L(s) ∼ λ Γ (λ ) sin(πλ/2)
π S1+λ (15)
The Lévy flight enables a balance between exploration and exploitation, which is crucial for avoiding local 
optima. The two-archive mechanism in MOCS2arc maintains two separate archives:
Convergence Archive: Stores high-quality solutions guiding the search towards Pareto front.
Diversity Archive: Preserves solution diversity by maintaining a diverse set of solutions.
The MOCS2arc algorithm is comprised of the following steps
Initialization
The algorithm starts via initializing a set of solutions randomly distributed in the search space. The initial 
population is evaluated, and non-dominated solutions are stored in the two archives.
Solution generation via Lévy flights
New solutions are generated using Lévy flights:
yi = xi + α + L(λ ) (16)
Fitness evaluation and archive update
The fitness of each solution is computed using objective functions. Solutions are stored based on their dominance 
in either CA or DA. With probability ( pa), poor solutions are discarded, and new solutions are introduced to 
maintain diversity. Steps 2 to 4 are repeated iteratively until a stopping criterion, such as a predefined number of 
iterations, is met33. Figure 2 demonstrates the flowchart of the MOCS2arc algorithm.
Results and discussion
Results of thermodynamic and exergoeconomic modelling
To analyse the proposed system from thermodynamic and thermoeconomic approaches, the simulations were 
used along with the Engineering software. The results obtained from the energy, exergy, and thermoeconomic 
analysis of the system are mentioned in Table 4..

As shown in Table 4., the system designed in this research is capable of supplying electrical power of 72.01 kW 
and cooling capacity of 56.83 kW. The energy efficiency of the combined system is 31.44%, which has increased 
by approximately 28% compared to the basic organic Rankine cycle. Moreover, the unit cost of the total exergy 
and the cost of the total exergy destruction are respectively 1259 dollars per gigajoule and 386,670 dollars per 
year. Figure 3 shows the destroyed exergy of the components that have the highest irreversibility. As observed, 
Condenser 1, due to its heat exchange with the external environment for cooling the turbine outlet flow, has the 
largest share of exergy destruction.
Results of thermoeconomic assessment
Table 5. indicates the outcomes of the thermoeconomic investigation of the combined facility. In this table, from 
right to left, the order is destruction cost, price, relative cost difference, and thermoeconomic factor.
Parametric study
Impact of combustion product temperature
Figure 4 demonstrates that as the temperature of the combustion products rises, both the basic cycle’s energy 
efficiency and the system’s overall energy efficiency improve. For instance, at 635 K, their efficiencies stand at 
26.91% and 35.72% respectively. By analysing these results and the graphic representation, it’s evident that the 
system’s overall energy efficiency sees an enhancement of roughly 30% when compared to the base ORC’s energy

efficiency. However, the exergy efficiency sees a reduction as the temperature increases. In line with the observed 
trend in energy efficiency, as combustion product temperatures rise, the power produced by the turbine and the 
heat supplied to the boiler also surge. Figure 4 depicts that with rising combustion product temperatures, the 
per-unit cost diminishes, while the total system exergy destruction rate amplifies. With elevated temperatures, 
there’s a boost in both the turbine power and the cooling capacity of the system, thereby incurring higher costs.

However, the aggregate per-unit cost of the entire system trends downwards. This drop can be attributed to the 
fact that factors raising the cost don’t escalate as sharply as other influential parameters.

Impact of condenser temperature
The condenser, known for its significant exergy destruction and high ratio of exergy wastage, is the focus of 
this section. Figure 5 showcases that, at a condenser temperature of 303.7 K, the entire system achieves its peak 
energy efficiency, registering at 33.44%. However, this efficiency drops as the temperature ascends. Concurrently, 
the system’s exergy efficiency bottoms out at 49.3% when the condenser temperature hits 307.2 K. Transitioning 
to Fig. 5, we observe a financial implication. As the condenser temperature elevates from 303.2 K to 310.2 K, the 
system’s unit cost climbs from 1259 to 1269 $/GJ. The rationale behind this uptick stems from the system’s cost 
dynamics. Based on the unit cost equation for the entire setup, both the net power output’s associated costs and 
those of the cooling capacity have swelled. This, in turn, prompts an upswing in the system’s cumulative per-unit 
cost.

Impact of steam generator temperature
The generator temperature is a key factor in the ejector refrigeration cycle. Its influence on the facility overall 
operation is the primary focus of this section. Figure 7 elucidates the effects of generator temperature changes 
on various performance indicators. According to Fig. 7, a hike in the generator temperature correlates with 
increases in both the thermodynamics efficiencies of the whole system, and these efficiencies move in tandem. 
As the generator temperature escalates, both the unit cost and the destructed exergy trend downwards. This 
decline can be attributed to the heightened generator temperature, which brings about reductions in the costs 
associated with the cooling capacity and the net power output. Consequently, this leads to a decrement in the 
overall per-unit cost for the system. Furthermore, as illustrated in the figure, there’s a decline in the system’s rate 
of exergy destruction.
The performance of the baseline ORC was simulated under identical inlet heat flux conditions (409.8 kW), 
and the results were as tabulated in Table 6..
This comparison clearly illustrates the 28% relative improvement in energy efficiency and a notable reduction 
in SUCP. The hybrid system not only produces more power but also introduces a cooling benefit, which the 
baseline ORC lacks.
Optimization results

The generated Pareto front effectively demonstrates the trade-off between exergy efficiency (ηexergy) and SUCP 
in an energy system optimization scenario. As observed in the scatter plot (see Fig.  8), increasing ηexergy
corresponds to a gradual reduction in SUCP, following an exponential decay trend. This behavior aligns with 
fundamental thermodynamic principles, where improvements in system efficiency lead to better utilization of 
energy inputs and cost reductions associated with energy losses. The knee point, marked in the Pareto front, 
represents the optimal compromise between cost and efficiency. It is identified at η exergy ≈ 64.88% and 
SUCP ≈ $902.21/GJ. This point is where the rate of cost reduction per unit efficiency gain diminishes, 
making it the most cost-effective operating condition. Beyond this point, additional efficiency gains come at 
a significantly higher cost, indicating diminishing returns. The Pareto front reveals a high-density region of 
optimal points around the knee, highlighting the stability of the cost-efficiency trade-off in this range. The 
broad spread of points indicates variability in cost and efficiency due to different parameter combinations. This

The exponential decay observed in the Pareto front suggests that initial improvements in efficiency yield

This trend is crucial for economic decision-making. From an engineering perspective, the Pareto front confirms

Conclusion
This investigation undertook an intricate energy, exergy, and economic exploration of a unique cycle aimed at 
concurrent power and cooling generation by fusing the ORC, ejector-based cooling, and a heat pipe. Grounded 
in the principles of the first and second laws of thermodynamics, this assessment employed the exhaust heat

from a marine diesel engine. The layered cycle, articulated through thermodynamic laws, revealed a surge in 
energy efficiency with augmented heat input to the boiler and elevated combustion product temperatures. While 
significant exergy losses were pinpointed in the ORC’s condenser and boiler, minor losses were attributed to the 
expansion valve and pump. This innovatively designed system promises an electrical output of approximately 
72.01 kW alongside a cooling provision of 56.83 kW. Demonstrating an impressive 31.44% energy efficiency, 
it trumps the basic ORC’s efficiency by nearly 28%. Integral to its design, the system’s heightened efficiency 
owes much to the negated need for a pump, courtesy of the heat pipe’s capillary action. Economic evaluations 
spotlighted a unit exergy cost of 1259 $/GJ and an annual exergy destruction cost of 386,670$. Furthermore, a 
meticulous investigation illuminated the repercussions of varied system parameters on overall performance. The 
key findings of this investigation are as follows:
(1) With an elevate in the exit temperature of combustion products entering the system, the overall energy 
efficiency has increased by ~30% compared to the energy efficiency of the basic ORC. Also, the exergetic 
efficacy has a decreasing trend with the increase in temperature.
(2) With an increase in condenser temperature within the specified range, the net output power reaches its 
minimum value of 71.81 kW at 307.1 K and then follows an upward trend. Also, the maximum cooling 
capacity of the entire system at the condenser temperature is 56.94 kW at 305.2 K.
